query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermomechanical treatment that induces a gradient nanohierarchical microstructure in the pristine CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will enable the in situ formation of adaptive, lubricious glaze layers during sliding, thereby maintaining a low coefficient of friction and wear rate from room temperature up to 800 °C under oxidizing conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Pristine CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Apply severe plastic deformation followed by a tailored annealing schedule to produce a gradient nanohierarchical microstructure with ultrafine grains and embedded nanoprecipitates.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted continuously from room temperature (~25 °C) to 800 °C under a constant normal load (e.g., 5–10 N) in an ambient/oxidizing atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: A gradient nanohierarchical surface layer comprising dual-scale features, including ultrafine grains and nanoprecipitates.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the engineered nanostructure facilitates multiple deformation mechanisms (e.g., dislocation motion, twinning) that progressively release gradient frictional stress; at elevated temperatures, it promotes rapid tribochemical reactions that form a dense, nanocrystalline glaze layer. This adaptive glaze minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear by providing a self-lubricating interface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline pristine alloy, the treated CoCrFeNi is expected to exhibit a consistently lower and more stable coefficient of friction along with a reduced wear rate across the full temperature range, from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The pristine CoCrFeNi alloy, when evaluated in sliding wear tests without microstructural modification, tends to develop unstable oxide layers and high friction/wear at elevated temperatures due to oxidation and microstructure instability.
generation.boundary: Test conditions are limited to a temperature range of approximately 25 °C to 800 °C, with constant sliding loads (around 5–10 N) and an ambient/oxidizing environment.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in friction and wear reduction will depend on the precise processing parameters and the kinetics of the in situ glaze formation, which may be sensitive to variations in sliding speed and load.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples: one set remains in the pristine state (control) and the other is processed via severe plastic deformation followed by a tailored annealing schedule to induce the gradient nanohierarchical microstructure. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests across a temperature ramp from room temperature to 800 °C under a constant load in an ambient/oxidizing atmosphere.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (CoF) as a function of temperature
Specific wear rate (wear volume per unit load and sliding distance) across the temperature range
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (e.g., using SEM, TEM, or XRD) to detect the formation and integrity of the lubricious glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction and wear rate over the entire temperature range compared to the control, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the formation of the adaptive glaze layer at high temperatures, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

For example, coherent B2 nanoprecipitates and nano-layered pearlitic structure allow accelerated formation of protective glaze layers on worn TiMoNb CCA [] and Fe44.5Co25.4Ni24.4Ti5.7 CCA [] at 600 °C, respectively, while the Zener’s pinning effect associated with the (hetero-)interfaces can effectively suppress grain coarsening caused by sliding and heating. Termed CCA or most famously as a subclass of these alloys known as high/medium-entropy alloys (H/MEAs), some of these alloys possess a variety of anomalous deformation mechanisms associated with multicomponent heterostructures, including saliently rugged local atomic-level pressures [], chemical short-range order [], spatially variable stacking faults (SFs) or twinning [,], severe lattice distortion [], and extraordinary dislocation reaction []. This offers the possibility for the alloy to progressively release gradient frictional stress through the competition and coexistence of multiple deformation pathways during sliding at low-to-moderate temperatures. Meanwhile, the broad compositional space of the CCA system allows us to integrate various oxidation-prone alloying elements into the alloy matrix for the formation of protec

Concurrently, the in situ formation of alumina nanoparticles and amorphous oxides further inhibits the grain coarsening by dissipating frictional energy. Therefore, the cooperative heterostructure in the NiX activates the dense nanocrystalline glaze layer during high-temperature wear, thus minimizing the adhesive and oxidative wear between the tribo-pairs. From the above analyses, the underlying wear mechanisms responsible for the unprecedented wear resistance in the NiX are schematically illustrated in Fig. S23. During sliding at RT, the intrinsic structures of NiX rely on multiple deformation pathways to evoke the NC tribo-layer and the UFG tribo-layer, thus progressively accommodating the gradient elastic–plastic deformation distributed along the friction interface. During sliding at 800 °C, the intrinsic structures of NiX are able to promote the formation of a dense glaze layer and a deformed tribo-layer containing alumina nanoparticles and amorphous oxides through spontaneous tribochemical reactions, which dramatically suppress adhesive and oxidative wear between tribo-pairs.

decision.trend: Early studies on high-entropy alloys targeted wear resistance by adding oxide dispersoids (e.g. Y2O3, PMC5706259) to improve strength and reduce wear at ambient conditions, but these attempts did not consistently lower friction over a wide temperature range. Subsequent work (PMC7311485) revealed that tailored near‐surface nanocrystalline or adaptive layers—formed via processing‐induced microstructure changes—can lower friction, though these were demonstrated in modified or slightly different HEA compositions and typically under inert environments. The most recent trend, as shown in PMC10241162, is to design a nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation that triggers in situ formation of adaptive, lubricious glaze layers during sliding; this approach successfully maintained ultralow wear rates from room temperature to 800 °C. However, these strategies have yet to be applied to the pristine CoCrFeNi system under ambient/oxidizing conditions.
decision.unsolved: The open challenge remains to modify the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy in a single, integrated manner so that during sliding under oxidizing conditions it autonomously develops a surface architecture that provides low friction and wear resistance across a very wide temperature span (room temperature to 800 °C).
decision.lever: Apply a controlled thermomechanical treatment (such as severe plastic deformation followed by tailored annealing) to induce a gradient nanohierarchical microstructure with dual-scale features (ultrafine grains with embedded nanoprecipitates).
decision.why: This intervention follows the emerging trend where engineered nanostructured surfaces create adaptive tribofilms during wear, as demonstrated in record PMC10241162. It is plausible to expect that inducing a gradient microstructure in the pristine CoCrFeNi matrix will prompt the in situ formation of a stable, lubricious glaze layer under sliding, thereby maintaining low friction and wear over the full range of test temperatures and addressing the limitations observed in previous trials.
